title: Lightweight IO handshake, pooled serializers, and affinity hints to reduce CPU request-path overhead
author: Amira Patel
description: Motivation: production load tests showed a persistent CPU hotpath on the request ingress where per-request serialization + thread-pin work and a short-lived mutex handshake cost ~1.8-3.6ms at p95 depending on load. This PR implements three coordinated changes to reduce that overhead: 1) a lightweight io-handshake protocol that replaces a mutex-and-syscall exchange between IO threads and worker executors with a lock-free single-writer ring handshake that eliminates syscall handoffs for the common path; 2) a pooled serializer object with small, thread-local arenas to avoid per-request heap allocations and repeated codec construction; and 3) a soft-affinity hinting layer for the worker scheduler that prefers socket-local workers but does not hard-pin threads, allowing the kernel to migrate when necessary and avoiding expensive sched_setaffinity calls on the hotpath. Design notes: the io-handshake is intentionally minimal: producers write a one-word descriptor and bump an epoch counter; consumers use an epoch-observed cursor and a memory-fence-based poll with exponential backoff. The serializer pool exposes try_acquire/try_release semantics; a fallback path constructs on demand but is rare in stress tests. Affinity hints are advisory only and used by the scheduler heuristics to prefer (not require) local queues; this removes the previous heavy-weight thread pin/unpin sequence that occurred per-request in corner cases. KV cache prefetching: as part of the same codepath we add a small heuristic to prefetch commonly hit tokens into the local worker's preallocated buffer for immediate KV lookup, which reduced remote cache miss amplification in our mixed-batch experiments. Continuous batching interaction: the handshake reduces enqueue-to-dequeue jitter so the continuous-batching timer can make tighter batch windows without sacrificing p95 latency; we tuned the batching gate to exploit the lower variance. Testing and benchmarking summary: microbenchmarks show median per-request CPU time on the hotpath decreased from 0.9ms to 0.37ms and p95 from 3.4ms to 1.6ms under the baseline inference load used by the perf lab. End-to-end throughput increased 12-18% under realistic multi-tenant workloads while p95 end-to-end latency decreased ~25% for small payloads. Safety and compatibility: changes are gated behind a runtime flag (runtime.enable_light_io_handshake) and default to on only in the 2026.02 rollout; we included feature flags to revert serializer pooling and affinity hints independently. Checklist: - [x] design doc and microbench proof-of-concept - [x] unit tests for handshake semantics and serializer pool - [x] integration tests with continuous batching enabled - [x] perf lab runs and dashboard updates - [x] feature-flag gating and rollout plan Rollout plan: merge as experimental behind flag, enable for dedicated hosts in canary pool, monitor token-level CPU and latency dashboards for regressions. Related: touches scheduling, kv-cache, and batching subsystems; references ENG-2419 and ENG-2490. TL;DR: fewer syscalls, fewer allocations, and softer affinity yields lower CPU consumption and more stable batch windows without breaking compatibility.
commits_summary: Initial implementation of lock-free io-handshake and epoch cursor (core logic + unit tests)
Serializer pool: thread-local free lists and fallback path; added small arena allocation for codecs
Scheduler: soft-affinity hint integration and heuristics changes to prefer socket-local queues
KV prefetch heuristic and small buffer management in worker hotpath
Batching: adjust continuous-batching gate to use reduced jitter and add telemetry
Tests: integration tests with high-concurrency harness and perf measurement scaffolding
Docs and changelog entry + feature flag gating
review_comments: Diego: Can you explain why you chose an epoch cursor vs sequence numbers? Concerned about ABA with wraparound.

Author (Amira): We use a 64-bit epoch and explicit wrap detection; the epoch is monotonic for the life of the process so ABA isn't a practical risk. Added comments and an assertion in the unit test to validate wrap handling in the simulated fast-producer scenario.
Leah: The serializer pool looks good, but I worry about memory usage explosion with many tenant contexts. Can we bound the pool size per worker?

Author (Amira): Added a soft cap per-worker that keeps up to N serializers (configurable via runtime.serializer_pool_max_per_worker). When exceeded we release least-recently-used objects to the global free list. Updated tests to cover the cap behavior.
Samir: CI flaked on test 'HighConcurrencyKVTest' on first run; looks like a timing sensitivity in the test harness.
Author (Amira): Fixed the test by adding a deterministic wait for the harness readiness signal instead of relying on a sleep; re-ran CI and it passed.
merge_commit_message:
squash: lightweight io handshake + serializer pool + affinity hints to cut CPU hotpath overhead

Reduces per-request syscall and allocation cost, improves continuous-batching stability, and adds a small KV prefetch heuristic. Gated behind runtime flags. See ENG-2419, ENG-2490.
release_notes: Performance: Reduce CPU request-path overhead by replacing mutex/sched handoffs with a lock-free handshake, introducing a pooled serializer to eliminate per-request allocations, and adding soft affinity hints. Expect ~12-18% throughput improvement and ~25% p95 latency reduction for small requests. Flag: runtime.enable_light_io_handshake.
